questions.prompt: On 1 July 2024, what sales growth does the point-in-time feature give, and why?
options: 14.58%, because June sales of 110 and revised March sales of 96 are the true figures
5.26%, because the June figure is not published until 25 July
10.00%, because June sales of 110 divided by March sales of 100 is 1.10
1.05%, because the revised March figure of 96 replaces 100
questions.explanation: On 1 July only the December (95) and March (100) figures are public, so growth is 100 / 95 - 1 = 5.26%. The June figure and the revision come later.

questions.prompt: A data file holds each quarter's final figure, dated by the quarter's last day. Why does shifting your signal by one bar not remove the look-ahead in it?
options: Because a shift only works on daily bars, not quarterly reports
Because the file has no publication dates, so the shift cannot be computed
Because the shift moves the signal, but the file's dates are already up to 25 days too early and its values include later revisions
Because revisions always make the figures larger, and a shift cannot undo that
questions.explanation: The file says June sales were known from 30 June and March sales were 96 all along. Both were learned later, so a one-bar shift is far too short and cannot undo a revision.

questions.prompt: A quarter ends on 30 June and its report is published on 25 July. What is the publication lag?
options: 0 days, because the sales happened by 30 June
It depends on when you download the data
questions.explanation: The publication lag is the time from the end of the period the number describes (30 June) to the day it becomes public (25 July): 25 days.
